questions.domain: Domain 1: Identify AI Concepts and Capabilities
questions.stem: A global logistics carrier wants an AI system that receives a delayed-shipment alert, autonomously queries carrier weather feeds, recalculates delivery SLAs, calls an ERP API to rebook freight capacity, and emails affected customers without human intervention at each intermediate step. Which AI workload paradigm best describes this capability?
options: Robotic Process Automation (RPA) executing fixed UI click macros.
Agentic AI orchestrating reasoning, memory, and multi-step tool execution.
Classical supervised regression forecasting transit duration from historical tables.
Single-turn extractive question answering over static SOP manuals.
questions.explanation: Option B is correct because Agentic AI systems combine a foundation model's reasoning with persistent state/memory and autonomous tool calling (APIs, search, code execution) to plan and complete multi-step goals dynamically. Option A fails because traditional RPA follows brittle, deterministic UI scripts and cannot reason over unstructured weather alerts or adapt plans when exceptions occur. Option C fails because supervised regression only outputs a numeric prediction rather than invoking external APIs or composing communications. Option D fails because single-turn extractive QA merely returns a text span from a document with no planning or action execution.
questions.use_case: Supply-chain operations teams build autonomous disruption-resolution agents in Azure AI Agent Service using OpenAPI tools for ERP rebooking and Grounding with Bing Search for live port and weather advisories.
questions.hack: Autonomous multi-step planning + calling external tools/APIs + adapting to intermediate results = Agentic AI.

questions.domain: Domain 2: Implement AI Solutions by Using Microsoft Foundry
questions.stem: An enterprise cloud platform team is onboarding three separate business units (Retail, Wealth Management, and Claims) into Microsoft Foundry. All three teams must share a centralized Private Link network topology, enterprise Azure Key Vault, and approved model connections, while keeping each team's prompt flows, evaluation runs, uploaded datasets, and developer RBAC strictly isolated. How should the team structure Microsoft Foundry?
options: Create one Foundry Project and place three Foundry Hubs inside it.
Create a single Foundry Hub and a single Foundry Project shared by all three business units.
Create one Foundry Hub for shared security, networking, and connections, and three separate Foundry Projects under that Hub.
Deploy three standalone Azure AI Services accounts without a Foundry Hub or Projects.
questions.explanation: Option C is correct because a Microsoft Foundry Hub is the top-level governance container that centralizes shared networking (VNet/Private Endpoints), compute, security settings, and external connections, while child Foundry Projects provide isolated workspaces for team-level assets, evaluations, files, and RBAC assignments. Option A fails because Hubs contain Projects, never the reverse. Option B fails because a single Project does not isolate prompt flows, datasets, or developer RBAC between business units. Option D fails because standalone AI Services accounts lack Foundry's unified project governance, evaluation, and agent workspace.
questions.use_case: Platform engineering teams provision one Hub per environment (dev/prod) via Bicep or Terraform and stamp out dedicated Foundry Projects for each product squad with scoped Azure AI Developer RBAC.
questions.hack: Foundry Hub = shared security, networking, compute, and connections; Foundry Project = isolated team workspace for assets, runs, and scoped RBAC.

questions.domain: Domain 1: Identify AI Concepts and Capabilities
questions.stem: During pre-release auditing of a retail bank's automated mortgage pre-qualification model, data scientists discover that applicants with identical credit scores and debt-to-income ratios receive 18% lower approval rates when their residential postal code historically correlates with lower-income neighborhoods. Which Microsoft Responsible AI principle is most directly violated?
options: Fairness.
Inclusiveness.
Transparency.
Privacy and Security.
questions.explanation: Option A is correct because Microsoft's Fairness principle requires AI systems to treat similarly situated people equitably and avoid allocative harm or proxy discrimination (such as postal codes acting as socioeconomic proxies in lending). Option B fails because Inclusiveness focuses on empowering diverse populations and accessibility (e.g., disabilities, languages, accents) rather than disparate lending outcomes for identical profiles. Option C fails because Transparency concerns disclosing how the system works and its limitations, not the underlying discriminatory disparity itself. Option D fails because Privacy and Security addresses protecting personal data confidentiality and defending against unauthorized access.
questions.use_case: Financial institutions evaluate tabular models with Fairlearn disparity metrics and remove proxy features like ZIP/postal codes before promoting lending models through governance gates.
questions.hack: Unequal outcomes or proxy bias affecting comparable individuals (loans, hiring, sentencing) = Fairness.

questions.domain: Domain 2: Implement AI Solutions by Using Microsoft Foundry
questions.stem: An aviation engineering firm using the Microsoft Foundry Model Catalog needs to deploy a single foundation model endpoint that inspects uploaded photographs of turbine blade cracks alongside maintenance PDFs and generates detailed inspection notes. Which model from the Foundry Model Catalog is the best fit for native vision-plus-text multimodal analysis?
options: text-embedding-3-large.
Cohere Rerank v3.
Whisper.
GPT-4o.
questions.explanation: Option D is correct because GPT-4o is a native multimodal foundation model in the Microsoft Foundry Model Catalog capable of reasoning jointly over images (such as turbine blade photos) and text instructions to generate structured inspection reports. Option A fails because text-embedding-3-large only converts text into numerical vectors for semantic search and cannot analyze images or generate text. Option B fails because Cohere Rerank reorders search results by relevance rather than processing images or writing prose. Option C fails because Whisper is an automatic speech-to-text audio transcription model.
questions.use_case: Field-service inspection apps send high-resolution equipment photos and checklist prompts to GPT-4o deployed in Microsoft Foundry to draft standardized maintenance work orders.
questions.hack: Native image + text multimodal reasoning in Foundry Model Catalog = GPT-4o (or Phi-4-multimodal for lightweight edge/SLM cases).

questions.domain: Domain 1: Identify AI Concepts and Capabilities
questions.stem: A commercial real-estate energy company has five years of historical hourly building data including outdoor temperature, occupancy count, HVAC setpoint, and the exact kilowatt-hours (kWh) consumed. The team wants a model that predicts tomorrow's exact continuous kWh demand for each building. Which machine learning technique should they use?
options: Binary classification.
K-Means clustering.
Supervised regression.
Named Entity Recognition.
questions.explanation: Option C is correct because predicting a continuous numerical value (exact kWh demand) from historical labeled features (temperature, occupancy, HVAC setpoint) is the textbook definition of supervised regression. Option A fails because binary classification predicts one of two discrete categories (such as outage vs. normal), not a continuous quantity. Option B fails because K-Means clustering is an unsupervised method used to group unlabeled observations rather than predict a known target number. Option D fails because Named Entity Recognition extracts entities from unstructured text.
questions.use_case: Smart-grid utilities train gradient-boosted regression models on weather and smart-meter histories to forecast 24-hour continuous energy load and optimize peak generation dispatch.
questions.hack: Historical labeled data + predicting a continuous number (price, kWh, temperature, revenue) = Supervised Regression.

questions.domain: Domain 2: Implement AI Solutions by Using Microsoft Foundry
questions.stem: A legal-tech startup is launching a pilot document-review tool in Microsoft Foundry that will serve 15 beta attorneys with sporadic daytime usage and zero traffic overnight or on weekends. The CTO wants to use Llama 3.3 with zero idle GPU infrastructure costs and no VM lifecycle management. Which Foundry deployment option should the team select?
options: Serverless API (Models-as-a-Service) pay-as-you-go deployment.
Provisioned Throughput Units (PTU) with an annual reservation.
Managed Compute online endpoint on dedicated NC-series GPU virtual machines.
On-premises Kubernetes cluster hosting manually quantized weights.
questions.explanation: Option A is correct because Microsoft Foundry Serverless API (pay-as-you-go) bills strictly per input and output token consumed, incurs zero idle compute cost overnight or on weekends, and requires zero VM patching or GPU quota management for supported partner models like Llama. Option B fails because PTU charges a continuous hourly/monthly reservation fee even when traffic is zero. Option C fails because Managed Compute provisions dedicated GPU VMs that bill per hour continuously regardless of idle time and require quota and instance sizing. Option D fails because self-hosting on-premises adds heavy infrastructure management overhead.
questions.use_case: Startups and internal pilot apps deploy Llama, Mistral, Cohere, and GPT models via Foundry Serverless API endpoints to validate product-market fit before committing to reserved capacity.
questions.hack: Sporadic/bursty traffic + zero idle cost + no VM management = Serverless API (pay-as-you-go).

questions.domain: Domain 1: Identify AI Concepts and Capabilities
questions.stem: A hospital network deploys an AI clinical triage assistant that suggests urgency levels from emergency-room intake notes. Engineering requires the system to undergo adversarial stress testing, reject out-of-distribution inputs safely, and automatically route any prediction with a confidence score below 0.90 directly to a senior triage nurse. Which Responsible AI principle do these controls primarily enforce?
options: Inclusiveness.
Privacy and Security.
Transparency.
Reliability and Safety.
questions.explanation: Option D is correct because Microsoft's Reliability and Safety principle mandates that AI systems perform dependably under both normal and unexpected conditions, undergo rigorous testing against edge cases, and include fail-safe human escalation mechanisms to prevent physical or clinical harm. Option A fails because Inclusiveness addresses broad accessibility and representation across diverse users. Option B fails because Privacy and Security focuses on data protection, encryption, and access control. Option C fails because Transparency focuses on communicating capabilities, limitations, and decision rationale to users.
questions.use_case: High-stakes healthcare and autonomous-vehicle teams enforce confidence thresholds, fallback escalation paths, and continuous drift monitoring to uphold Reliability and Safety.
questions.hack: Fail-safes, confidence cutoffs, human escalation, edge-case testing, preventing harm = Reliability and Safety.

questions.domain: Domain 2: Implement AI Solutions by Using Microsoft Foundry
questions.stem: A regulated European retail bank is hardening its production Microsoft Foundry Hub and Azure OpenAI deployments before a security audit. The bank's zero-trust standard prohibits static shared secrets in application code and forbids inference traffic from traversing the public internet. Which TWO security controls should the architect implement? (Select TWO.)
options: Authenticate workloads with Microsoft Entra ID Managed Identities and RBAC roles while disabling local API key authentication.
Store the primary Azure OpenAI API key inside a public GitHub Actions variable for rapid CI/CD rotation.
Configure Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) to allow wildcard origins (*) on the inference endpoint.
Attach Azure Private Endpoints to the Foundry Hub, Azure OpenAI, and Azure AI Search resources inside a private VNet.
Grant the Subscription Owner role to every frontend web container so it never hits authorization errors.
questions.explanation: Options A and D are correct because Microsoft Entra ID Managed Identities with least-privilege RBAC (plus disableLocalAuth=true) eliminate static shared secrets completely, and Azure Private Endpoints route all inference and RAG traffic over private Microsoft backbone IPs inside the bank's VNet with public network access disabled. Option B fails because storing keys in CI/CD variables still relies on static keys and risks secret leakage. Option C fails because wildcard CORS widens browser exposure rather than blocking public internet routing. Option E fails because granting Subscription Owner violates least privilege.
questions.use_case: Enterprise landing zones pair disableLocalAuth=true, Managed Identities (Cognitive Services OpenAI User), and Private Link DNS zones across Foundry Hubs and connected AI Services.
questions.hack: Zero-trust Foundry production = Entra ID Managed Identity (no API keys) + Azure Private Endpoints (no public internet).

questions.domain: Domain 1: Identify AI Concepts and Capabilities
questions.stem: An online retailer has 2.4 million customer records containing annual spend, return rate, and browse frequency, but no predefined marketing persona labels exist in the database. The analytics team wants an algorithm to discover natural customer groupings automatically. Which machine learning approach should they apply?
options: Supervised multiclass classification.
Unsupervised clustering.
Supervised linear regression.
Extractive text summarization.
questions.explanation: Option B is correct because unsupervised clustering algorithms (such as K-Means or DBSCAN) discover inherent groupings in unlabeled datasets based on feature similarity without requiring historical target labels. Option A fails because multiclass classification is supervised and requires pre-labeled training categories. Option C fails because linear regression is supervised and predicts a continuous target variable from labeled history. Option D fails because extractive summarization operates on text documents, not tabular behavioral segmentation.
questions.use_case: Marketing teams run K-Means clustering on RFM (Recency, Frequency, Monetary) customer metrics to uncover natural buyer personas before designing targeted retention campaigns.
questions.hack: No historical labels + discover natural groups/segments = Unsupervised Clustering.

questions.domain: Domain 2: Implement AI Solutions by Using Microsoft Foundry
questions.stem: A Tier-1 credit card issuer runs a 24/7 real-time fraud-advisory copilot backed by GPT-4o in Microsoft Foundry. The contact center generates a steady baseline of 450,000 tokens per minute and contractually requires deterministic sub-second time-to-first-token latency with dedicated reserved throughput immune to multi-tenant noisy-neighbor spikes. Which deployment tier should the architect choose?
options: Standard pay-as-you-go serverless deployment.
Batch API asynchronous processing deployment.
Provisioned Throughput Units (PTU).
Free F0 evaluation tier.
questions.explanation: Option C is correct because Provisioned Throughput Units (PTU) allocate dedicated, reserved model processing capacity in Microsoft Foundry, delivering predictable low-latency P99 performance and guaranteed token throughput for steady high-volume production workloads. Option A fails because Standard pay-as-you-go shares multi-tenant capacity pools and can experience variable latency or 429 throttling during peak global load. Option B fails because Batch API targets offline asynchronous jobs with up to 24-hour completion SLAs, not real-time contact centers. Option D fails because Free tiers have tiny rate limits unsuitable for production.
questions.use_case: High-volume contact centers purchase PTU reservations for baseline steady traffic and configure Azure API Management to spill unexpected burst overflow onto a Standard pay-as-you-go pool.
questions.hack: Guaranteed low latency + reserved capacity + steady high TPM = Provisioned Throughput Units (PTU).

questions.domain: Domain 1: Identify AI Concepts and Capabilities
questions.stem: A junior ML engineer prepares a churn dataset by computing the mean and standard deviation across the entire 100,000-row table to normalize numeric features, and only afterward splits the table into an 80% training set and a 20% validation set. Why is this preprocessing sequence problematic?
options: It introduces data leakage because statistical information from the validation set influenced training feature scaling, inflating evaluation scores.
It causes underfitting because 80% of the data is insufficient to train any binary classifier.
It converts a supervised classification task into an unsupervised clustering task.
It prevents the model from computing a confusion matrix on the validation set.
questions.explanation: Option A is correct because fitting scalers, imputers, or encoders on the full dataset before splitting leaks distribution statistics from the held-out validation rows into the training pipeline, creating overly optimistic validation performance that degrades in production. Option B fails because an 80/20 split on 100,000 rows provides plenty of training samples and does not inherently cause underfitting. Option C fails because feature scaling does not remove target labels or turn supervised learning into clustering. Option D fails because confusion matrices depend only on predicted vs. actual labels.
questions.use_case: ML pipelines encapsulate scaling and imputation inside scikit-learn Pipeline objects fit strictly on X_train, then call transform() on X_val and X_test to prevent leakage.
questions.hack: Always split FIRST, then fit scalers/imputers ONLY on the training split to prevent data leakage.

questions.domain: Domain 2: Implement AI Solutions by Using Microsoft Foundry
questions.stem: A Python microservice running on Azure Container Apps currently calls a Microsoft Foundry inference endpoint using a hardcoded subscription key stored in an environment file. The security team mandates migrating to passwordless authentication that works seamlessly both on developers' local machines (via Azure CLI login) and in production Container Apps (via Managed Identity) without code changes. Which credential class should the team use?
options: AzureKeyCredential loaded from a local .env file.
DefaultAzureCredential from the azure-identity SDK backed by Microsoft Entra ID RBAC.
SharedAccessSignatureCredential generated from Azure Blob Storage.
BasicAuthCredential passing a username and password header.
questions.explanation: Option B is correct because DefaultAzureCredential from azure-identity automatically chains Entra ID authentication mechanisms, using Managed Identity in Azure Container Apps and Azure CLI/VS Code credentials during local development with zero secrets in code. Option A fails because AzureKeyCredential requires managing and rotating static API keys. Option C fails because SAS tokens apply to Azure Storage access, not Foundry model inference auth. Option D fails because Basic Auth with username/password is unsupported and insecure for Azure AI endpoints.
questions.use_case: Cloud-native Python services instantiate ChatCompletionsClient(endpoint=..., credential=DefaultAzureCredential()) and assign the Cognitive Services User or Azure AI Developer RBAC role to the Container App's user-assigned Managed Identity.
questions.hack: Passwordless local-dev + production Managed Identity auth in Azure SDKs = DefaultAzureCredential + Entra ID RBAC.

questions.domain: Domain 1: Identify AI Concepts and Capabilities
questions.stem: An insurance analytics team is building a supervised machine learning classifier to predict whether vehicle claims require special fraud investigation. Which option arranges the four lifecycle stages in the correct sequential order from start to production?
options: Order 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4: (1) Train model on full dataset -> (2) Deploy endpoint to production -> (3) Split historical data into train and test sets -> (4) Compute validation precision and recall.
Order 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4: (1) Evaluate confusion matrix on test split -> (2) Clean and split labeled data -> (3) Fit model parameters on training split -> (4) Monitor production data drift.

Order 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4: (1) Clean labeled historical data and split into training, validation, and test sets -> (2) Fit preprocessing transforms and train the classifier strictly on the training split -> (3) Evaluate generalization metrics (Precision, Recall, F1) on the held-out validation/test splits -> (4) Deploy the validated model to production and continuously monitor accuracy and data drift.
Order 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4: (1) Deploy baseline model to production -> (2) Collect training labels after deployment -> (3) Skip validation evaluation -> (4) Fit feature scalers on test data.
questions.explanation: Option C is correct because a disciplined supervised ML workflow always cleans and splits data first (Step 1), fits transforms and trains strictly on the training split to avoid leakage (Step 2), verifies generalization on held-out validation/test splits (Step 3), and only then deploys with ongoing drift monitoring (Step 4). Option A fails because training on the full dataset before splitting causes severe data leakage and deploys an unvalidated model. Option B fails because you cannot evaluate a confusion matrix before preparing data and training the model. Option D fails because deploying without training or validation is unsafe and violates ML engineering fundamentals.
questions.use_case: MLOps pipelines automate these exact four gates in Azure Machine Learning / Foundry so no model registers to production without passing held-out test-set threshold checks.
questions.hack: Supervised ML sequence: Split First -> Train on Train Split -> Evaluate on Held-Out Split -> Deploy & Monitor Drift.

questions.domain: Domain 2: Implement AI Solutions by Using Microsoft Foundry
questions.stem: A healthcare clearinghouse integrates a legacy third-party claims engine that only supports API-key authentication (it cannot acquire Microsoft Entra ID OAuth tokens) when calling Azure AI Document Intelligence. The security officer requires automated 90-day secret rotation, full audit logging of secret reads, and private network connectivity with no public endpoint exposure. What architecture satisfies all constraints?
options: Embed the Document Intelligence key in an encrypted JSON file committed to a private Git repository.
Expose Document Intelligence on a public endpoint restricted only by a static API key header.
Disable HTTPS TLS encryption so the legacy claims engine can connect directly over HTTP.
Store and rotate the Document Intelligence API key inside Azure Key Vault with RBAC audit logging, and route calls over Azure Private Endpoints.
questions.explanation: Option D is correct because when legacy clients cannot use Entra ID directly, storing API keys in Azure Key Vault provides centralized secret management, automated rotation support, and audit trails, while Azure Private Endpoints keep all Document Intelligence traffic off the public internet. Option A fails because committing secrets to Git (even encrypted in a private repo) violates secret-management hygiene and breaks automated rotation. Option B fails because a public endpoint violates the private network requirement. Option C fails because disabling TLS exposes sensitive PHI in plaintext and is rejected by Azure endpoints.
questions.use_case: Hybrid enterprises bridge legacy ERP/claims integrations to Azure AI Services using Azure Key Vault secrets referenced at runtime plus ExpressRoute and Private Link endpoints.
questions.hack: Legacy client requires API key (cannot use Entra ID) -> Store & rotate key in Azure Key Vault + Private Endpoint.

questions.domain: Domain 1: Identify AI Concepts and Capabilities
questions.stem: A telecom data scientist trains a deep decision-tree model to predict broadband router failures. After training, the model achieves 99.4% accuracy on the training set but only 61.2% accuracy on the held-out validation set. Which phenomenon is occurring, and which remediation is most appropriate?
options: Underfitting; increase maximum tree depth and remove all regularization constraints.
Overfitting; constrain model complexity (such as limiting tree depth or adding regularization) and gather more diverse training data.
Class balance perfection; deploy the model immediately because training accuracy exceeds 99%.
Label encoding error; switch from classification to K-Means clustering.
questions.explanation: Option B is correct because a massive gap between near-perfect training accuracy (99.4%) and poor validation accuracy (61.2%) is the classic signature of overfitting (high variance), where the model memorized noise in the training samples; reducing complexity (pruning/max depth, regularization, dropout) and adding diverse training data improves generalization. Option A fails because underfitting shows poor performance on BOTH training and validation sets, and increasing depth makes overfitting worse. Option C fails because deploying an overfitted model causes severe production errors. Option D fails because clustering does not fix high variance in a supervised failure predictor.
questions.use_case: Predictive maintenance engineers inspect train-vs-validation learning curves and apply tree pruning, L2 regularization, and cross-validation to eliminate overfitting before rollout.
questions.hack: High train score + low validation score = Overfitting (memorized noise) -> Regularize / simplify model / add more data.
